segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to his attendants,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him away in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for John had been telling him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And although he wanted to kill him, he feared the crowd, because they regarded him as a prophet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Herod’s birthday celebration came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so much that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Prompted by her mother, she said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give me, here on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The king was distressed, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests he ordered it to be given,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples came and took away the corpse and buried him, and they went and told Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a remote place by himself. But the crowds heard of it and followed him on foot from the towns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them and healed their sick.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, the disciples approached him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is a remote place, and the hour is already late. Send the crowds away, so that they can go into the villages and buy themselves food.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Bring them here to me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he ordered the crowds to recline on the grass. He took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven and said the blessing; then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces: twelve baskets full.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After sending the crowds away, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The boat was already a long way from the land, battered by the waves, for the wind was against it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is a ghost!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cried out in fear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But at once Jesus spoke to them:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Peter got down from the boat, walked on the waters, and came toward Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But seeing the strong wind, he became afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, save me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they got into the boat, the wind dropped.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those in the boat bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly you are God’s Son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The men of that place recognized him and sent word throughout that whole surrounding region, and people brought to him all who were ill,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him to let them touch just the fringe of his cloak. And all who touched it were made well.

notes.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Roman oversight. 'Tetrarch' was the title of a ruler of part of a divided kingdom and ranked below a king.

notes.phrase: the wife of his brother Philip
notes.note: Herodias had left her first husband, a half-brother of Antipas, to marry Antipas. Jewish law forbade marrying a brother's wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21), which is the basis of John's charge in verse 4. Josephus calls the first husband simply Herod; whether he also bore the name Philip is disputed.
Antipas never officially held the title of king, and Matthew has called him tetrarch in verse 1. 'King' here reflects popular usage for a local ruler rather than his formal rank.

The Greek verb means to lie back or recline, the normal posture at a meal in the first century. Most translations say 'sit down', which is the modern equivalent but loses the suggestion that the crowd is being arranged as for a meal.

The Greek verb has no object here. Some translations supply one, so that Jesus blesses the loaves; others render it 'gave thanks'. The Jewish custom at meals was to bless God for the food, and that is the more likely sense, though the Greek does not settle it.

notes.phrase: a long way from the land
notes.traditional: in the midst of the sea
notes.note: The Greek says the boat was 'many stadia' from land. A stadion was roughly 185 metres (about 600 feet), so the distance is probably a few miles. Other manuscripts read 'in the middle of the sea', as in Mark's account, and older English versions follow that reading.

notes.phrase: the fourth watch of the night
notes.traditional: the fourth watch of the night
notes.note: On the Roman reckoning the night was divided into four watches. The fourth ran from about three in the morning until dawn, so the disciples had been struggling at sea for most of the night.

The Greek is literally 'I am', the ordinary way of saying 'It's me'. The same words are also God's self-designation in the Greek Old Testament (for example in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10). Many interpreters hear that echo here, in a scene where Jesus walks on the sea as God does in Job 9:8; the plain sense of self-identification is certain, the further resonance is likely but debated.
Some important early manuscripts lack the word 'strong' and read simply 'seeing the wind'. The edition translated here includes it; the sense is little affected either way.

The Greek verb denotes the act of bowing or prostrating oneself in homage, whether before a god, a king or a superior. Most translations render it 'worshiped' here, and the accompanying confession shows that the homage is of the highest kind. The rendering keeps the physical act the word describes and lets the confession carry its meaning.

The word can mean the edge of a garment, but it is also the term for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment in obedience to Numbers 15:38–39. Matthew uses it for those tassels in 23:5, so that is probably what is meant here.

candidates.reason: Used across the Gospels and Revelation for homage ranging from respect to worship; the choice between 'worship' and 'bow down' must be made consistently and by stated criteria.
Recurs throughout the Synoptics of Jesus and in parables, and translations vary between 'had compassion', 'felt pity' and 'was moved'.
The plural shifts between 'miracles', 'mighty works' and 'powers' across the Gospels and Paul, and readers should see one consistent treatment per sense.
At meal scenes (the feedings, the Last Supper, Emmaus) translations vary between 'blessed', 'blessed it' and 'gave thanks', which obscures the links between these passages.
A characteristic Matthean term whose rendering depends on the register decision for πίστις (faith or trust) and should match it everywhere.
